item.title: Partially Identified Ambiguity
item.description: arXiv:2602.07634v3 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper addresses the normative question of whether one should condition on the data when performing robust Bayesian analysis under partial identification. We provide an ex ante representation of the conditional Gamma-minimax criterion and show that it can violate Aumann plausibility, a set-valued generalization of the rational expectations property. Our main characterization result establishes that Aumann plausibility holds if and only if the decision maker's prior set exhibits partially identified ambiguity. The latter condition requires the prior set to equal the Aumann expectation of a random set of distributions supported on the parameter's identified sets. We interpret these results as suggesting that conditional Gamma-minimax should only be used under partially identified ambiguity. The implications for various robust Bayesian methods are discussed.
item.dc:creator: Cheaheon Lim

item.title: Inference for Linear Systems with Unknown Coefficients
item.description: arXiv:2604.24904v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper considers the problem of testing whether there exists a solution satisfying known linear constraints to a linear system of equations. Importantly and in contrast to some prior work, we allow all parameters in the system of equations, including the slope coefficients, to be unknown. For this reason, we describe the linear system as having unknown (as opposed to known) coefficients. This hypothesis testing problem arises naturally when constructing confidence sets for possibly partially identified parameters in the analysis of nonparametric instrumental variables models, treatment effect models, and random coefficient models, among other settings. We begin our analysis by providing a novel characterization of the set of coefficient pairs for which the linear system is feasible. Leveraging this characterization, we develop a testing procedure based on sample splitting. We establish its validity under weak and interpretable conditions on the linear system. An important feature of these conditions is that they permit the dimensionality of the problem to grow rapidly with the sample size. A further attractive property of our test is that it does not require simulation to compute suitable critical values. We illustrate the practical relevance of our theoretical results in a simulation study.
item.dc:creator: Yuehao Bai, Kirill Ponomarev, Andres Santos, Azeem M. Shaikh, Max Tabord-Meehan, Alexander Torgovitsky

item.title: Recovering Direct Price Effects of Environmental Amenities in Housing Markets: Regression and Causal Machine Learning Model Assessment with Empirical Monte Carlo Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2606.02795v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hedonic price models are widely used to value environmental amenities, yet practical guidance for estimating direct unconfounded price effects remains sparse. We conduct an empirical Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate traditional regression and causal machine learning (CML) approaches for estimating the direct unmediated price effect of spatially delineated amenities on treated properties (DUET), a lower-bound approximation of welfare change with direct applications to benefit-cost analysis. Whereas previous simulations rely on parametric assumptions, we preserve the actual data-generating process underlying over 1 million property transactions from upstate New York (1990--2024) and randomly assign treatment locations across iterations, establishing a ground truth against which estimation error can be measured precisely. Generalized difference-in-differences (DID) regression consistently outperforms baseline DID and two-way fixed effects models across all scenarios. Causal forest DID performs comparably to generalized DID in most scenarios and, in larger samples (at least 3,000 treated observations) increasingly common in contemporary hedonic studies, achieves significantly lower estimation error and better confidence interval coverage. Its advantage widens further when the treatment induces a nonlinear shift in the hedonic price function. The performance of causal forest DID, however, hinges on specification choices that differ from regression practice, such as including geographic attributes only in the price models and avoiding high-dimensional fixed effects. We translate these findings into method-specific best-practice recommendations for both regression and CML approaches.
item.dc:creator: Zhenshan Chen (Virginia Tech), Matthew Mair (Virginia Tech), Klaus Moeltner (Virginia Tech)

item.title: Learning Where to Look: The Geometry of Data Combination and Collection
item.description: arXiv:2607.04885v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large datasets covering populations in the status quo are becoming increasingly available, while interventions can usually be rolled out only to small selected samples. How can these two sources of information be combined to estimate the effect on untreated units? And who should be treated next to improve estimation the most? I focus on matching estimators and shed light on both problems, drawing from results in computational geometry. First, I prove that interpolation over the Delaunay simplex minimizes worst-case bias at any untreated unit, given any treated sample. Second, I show the collection problem has a geometric representation that yields significant reductions in worst-case bias with few additions (80% with 20 additions in an empirical application), leading to sizeable cost-efficiency gains in collection plans.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Opocher

item.title: Estimating a Rational Inattention Discrete Choice Model: A Semiparametric Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.18479v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: People's choices depend on both the payoffs of the available options and what they learn about those payoffs before deciding. This paper shows how choice data identify both unobserved payoff heterogeneity and the cost of information acquisition in a rational inattention discrete-choice model. I establish conditions for semiparametric point identification using exogenous payoff and information-cost shifters, without imposing parametric forms on the taste-shock distribution or on how the unit cost of information varies with observed characteristics. In the model with binary choice, I construct an unobserved choice threshold whose cumulative distribution function is the choice probability as a function of the payoff shifter. Moments of this threshold identify the payoff coefficients and the unit cost of information at each value of the information-cost shifter. A deconvolution argument then identifies the taste-shock distribution. I then extend identification to the model with multinomial choice. To estimate the model, I propose a sieve minimum-distance estimator based on observed market shares and establish its consistency. For inference, I construct confidence regions by test inversion because binding parameter constraints can make the estimator's limiting distribution nonnormal. In an application to Amazon Mechanical Turk, model counterfactuals show that lower unit costs of information raise the average task-taking probability and reduce wage elasticity.
item.dc:creator: Hanqi Wang

item.title: Randomization Tests in Randomized Saturation Designs
item.description: arXiv:2607.04257v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Randomized saturation designs are widely used to study spillover effects in clustered populations. In these designs, clusters are first assigned to treatment saturation levels, and units are then randomized within clusters according to the assigned saturation. This paper develops randomization tests for such experiments under several null hypotheses that arise naturally in spillover analysis. We first compare each unit's untreated potential outcomes at two saturation levels: the partially sharp null requires zero spillover for every unit, while the bounded null imposes a prespecified upper bound on each unit's spillover effect. Both hypotheses can be tested using a common conditional randomization framework that provides finite-sample validity. We next develop a finite-sample valid unconditional randomization test of whether each unit's untreated potential outcome is nondecreasing across saturation levels. Finally, we study weak average-spillover nulls and show that our conditional randomization framework delivers asymptotically valid inference using studentized statistics. Simulations and an application to the Zomba Cash Transfer experiment illustrate the finite-sample behavior and practical implementation of the methods.
item.dc:creator: Jizhou Liu, Azeem M. Shaikh, Liang Zhong

item.title: Forecasting Realized Volatility with Time Series Foundation Models: A Comparison with Econometric Benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2607.05291v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained on large collections of series and forecast a new series without being trained on it. We compare nine TSFMs, used in this zero-shot setting, with eight econometric models, including the Heterogeneous Autoregressive (HAR) family. We forecast the realized volatility of 50 assets in equities, currencies and futures from the VOLARE dataset one, five and 22 days ahead, and compare the forecasts with pairwise and multi-model tests. The foundation models do not outperform the econometric benchmarks as a class. Only Tiny Time Mixers (TTM), the smallest of them, has a lower average QLIKE loss than the logarithmic HAR (Log-HAR) at every tested horizon, by a narrow margin. For most assets, the Model Confidence Set (MCS) contains TTM together with Log-HAR and several other models. Accuracy differs far more across the foundation models than between the best of them and Log-HAR, so which foundation model one chooses matters more than whether one uses a foundation model or an econometric one. For an investor who targets a constant volatility, TTM's edge is worth a few basis points a year before trading costs. Since TTM and Log-HAR make different errors, their equal-weight average matches the best single model and enters the MCS for nearly every asset.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Brini

item.title: Optimal Uniform Pricing for Multi-Interval Dispatch without Make-Whole Uplifts
item.description: arXiv:2609.00541v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In a network with ramp-limited generators and inaccurate net-demand forecasts, practical rolling-window dispatch can drive locational marginal prices (LMPs) below generators' bid-in offers. In such cases, out-of-market (OOM) settlements are used to compensate generators and maintain dispatch-following incentives, but OOM can have negative consequences, including nontransparent real-time price signals, discriminatory compensation, and incentives for untruthful bidding. This paper presents an optimal uniform pricing rule that minimizes demand payments, eliminates OOM make-whole payments, preserves LMP-based congestion charges, and ensures revenue adequacy. We derive the proposed pricing rule in closed form and relate it to existing pricing schemes. Numerical comparisons demonstrate favorable generator profits and reduced price volatility. However, higher generator profits are accompanied by increased demand payments, reflecting the in-market, uniform allocation of ramping costs while preserving the LMP-based congestion charges widely used in real-time market settlements. The numerical results also show that, under LMP with OOM settlement, a price-taking generator has an incentive to inflate its offer, whereas this incentive is absent under the proposed pricing rule within the tested bid range.
item.dc:creator: Valentina Norambuena-Guzman, Cong Chen, Lang Tong, Timothy D. Mount
